plan.topic: Plague testing explained: what 'presumptive' vs 'confirmed' plague means under CDC's 2020 case definition, and why confirmation can take days
plan.angle: Hook: 'Plague tests: why can confirming it take days?' Context line (one sentence): 'As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO says a key uncertainty in the Irkutsk oblast death is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis.' Then settled science only: under CDC's 2020 case definition, PCR, antigen or F1 rapid tests make a case presumptive or probable; confirmed means Y. pestis grown in culture or a fourfold change in antibody levels between samples. Culture and paired antibody tests take time, which is why clinicians start antibiotics before results are back when plague is suspected. Close: possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently; 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Title: 'Plague Tests: Why Confirming It Can Take Days (CDC) #shorts'.

plan.why: It answers today's top new search question (NYT, Oct 10) with settled CDC definitions and no speculation. Low competition, and it doubles as the playbook's 35–50 s length test. | fact-check: The topic is settled science and on-format: a plain question, an agency named, and 'Plague' as the first word. Swap the context line for the primary-source wording: WHO DON620 (Oct 10, 2026) says 'A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.' Don't use 'WHO said the cause is still unclear' from news paraphrase. Follow the craft-note rules: PCR, antigen and F1 rapid tests = 'presumptive/probable'; 'confirmed' = Y. pestis isolated in culture or a fourfold change in antibody titer. Cite the CDC/CSTE case definition page itself (NNDSS Plague 2020 case definition), not the 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis' page. Don't give specific culture turnaround hours unless a cited source states them. Antibody fourfold rises need paired samples taken weeks apart. Say 'can take days or longer' rather than a fixed figure. Don't imply that any specific test was or wasn't done in the Irkutsk case. 35–50 s is fine.

package.description:
Quick answer: As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO lists the Irkutsk oblast lab worker's death as pneumonia of undetermined etiology; a confirmed diagnosis is still missing and a lab-associated exposure can't be fully excluded. Under CDC's 2020 case definition, PCR/antigen tests are presumptive, and lab confirmation takes time. Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
- CDC NNDSS/CSTE, "Plague 2020 Case Definition" – https://ndc.services.cdc.gov/case-definitions/plague-2020/

- CDC, "Clinical Care of Plague" (updated May 15, 2024) – https://www.cdc.gov/plague/hcp/clinical-care/index.html

social.instagram_caption:
As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO lists the Irkutsk oblast lab worker's death as pneumonia of undetermined etiology, with no confirmed diagnosis (WHO Disease Outbreak News). So why isn't a positive plague test always "confirmed"?

Here's what the testing actually means, under CDC's 2020 case definition:
• PCR, antigen and F1 tests = "presumptive"
• That plus a sick patient with no link to a known case or exposure, and no other diagnosis = "probable"
• That plus a link to a known case or exposure = can count as "confirmed"
• Lab confirmation needs Y. pestis grown in culture plus a second test, or a fourfold or greater rise or fall in F1 antibodies across 2 blood samples, the second taken later in the illness

That's why confirming takes time. But CDC says don't wait: start treatment as soon as plague is suspected.

Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.

Save this for the next plague headline you see.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

factcheck.summary:
The science holds up, but the script needs 3 fixes before it goes out. It runs about 230 words against our 170-word limit, scene s2 leaves out one development from WHO's Oct 10 report, and s3 needs its link wording tightened.

What checks out:
- **CDC 2020 case definition (S1):**
  - Presumptive: PCR, DFA, IHC or antigen tests, including F1, or a raised F1 antibody level.
  - Confirmatory: culture checked by a second test, or a fourfold or greater change in paired F1 antibody results.
  - Probable: presumptive result, no epidemiologic link and no alternative diagnosis.
  - Confirmed: confirmatory result, or a presumptive result plus an epidemiologic link.
- **WHO's Oct 10, 2026 report (DON620, S2):** the s2 quote card is word for word ("A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker."). The Oct 6 and Oct 7–8 statements, "has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission" and "cannot be fully excluded" are all accurate.
- **CDC Clinical Care page (S6):** it says "Begin appropriate therapy as soon as plague is suspected" and "DO NOT WAIT FOR DIAGNOSTIC TEST RESULTS IF YOU SUSPECT PLAGUE". Updated May 15, 2024.
- **CDC Signs and Symptoms page (S4):** it lists fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain for pneumonic plague (plus headache and weakness). Updated May 15, 2024.

Safety: the urgent-contact line and the worried line are both present, and nothing suggests self-treatment.

A search on Oct 12 found nothing newer than WHO's Oct 10 report. Re-check WHO and Rospotrebnadzor at publish time.

issues.claim: On Oct 6, Russian authorities told WHO no case of plague had been registered recently in Irkutsk oblast, and on Oct 7–8 that tests on the patient and contacts were reportedly negative for high-threat pathogens.
issues.problem: The status is incomplete. WHO's Oct 10 report also says: "The authorities further reported that the fatality was not due to plague infection." Our rules say to include every dated development. This one matters most in a video about how plague tests work. The line is about 77 words long and is the main reason the Short is over its word limit.
issues.fix: Replace the s2 narration with: "As of Oct 10, 2026, WHO lists the death of a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast as pneumonia of undetermined etiology. On Oct 6, Russian authorities told WHO no plague case had been registered recently there. On Oct 7–8, they said tests on the patient and contacts were reportedly negative for high-threat pathogens, and they reported the death was not due to plague. WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission, but says a confirmed diagnosis is still missing and a lab-associated exposure can't be fully excluded."

issues.problem: The narration is about 228 words, or about 236 if the save CTA is spoken. Our limit for Shorts is 170 words, including the status line. It still fits under the 178-second hard limit, but our rules say to cut a beat rather than run long.
issues.fix: Use the trimmed s2 wording above. Then change s5 to: "Here's the catch: culture means growing the bacteria, then a second test. The antibody route needs a second blood sample, taken later." Change s3 to: "Under CDC's 2020 case definition, PCR or antigen tests, including F1, are presumptive. Alone, that's a probable case. Linked to a confirmed case or a known plague area, it can count as confirmed." Shorten s7 to: "Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently." Then end on the CTA, which already carries the worried line.

issues.claim: In a sick patient with no link to a known case or exposure, and no other diagnosis, that's a probable case. / 'probable case unless linked to a known case or exposure'
issues.problem: CDC's definition of an epidemiologic link is narrower than "a known case or exposure". It covers 3 things: a link within the prior 2 weeks to a person or animal with confirmatory lab evidence, close contact with a confirmed pneumonic case, or living in or travel to an area with confirmed plague activity in fleas or animals. "Exposure" is too broad. The on-screen 'fact' line also drops the requirement that the patient's illness looks like plague (clinically compatible) and has no alternative diagnosis.
issues.fix: In the narration, write "no link to a confirmed case or a known plague area" instead of "no link to a known case or exposure". Change the myth_fact fact to: "Presumptive on their own. In a plague-like illness with no other diagnosis, that's a probable case; linked to a confirmed case or a known plague area, it can count as confirmed (CDC 2020 case definition)".

issues.claim: the antibody route needs a second blood sample taken later in the illness
issues.problem: CDC says "paired serum", which is usually an early sample and a later recovery-phase sample. That second sample may be taken after the illness, not during it. "Later in the illness" narrows what the source says.
issues.fix: Write "needs a second blood sample, taken later", as in the list item "Antibodies: a 2nd blood sample, later".

issues.claim: So CDC says: start treatment as soon as plague is suspected. Don't wait for results.
issues.problem: CDC's wording is guidance for clinicians. It shouldn't read as advice to viewers, who aren't being told to treat themselves.
issues.fix: Write: "So CDC tells clinicians: begin treatment as soon as plague is suspected. Don't wait for test results."

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: The fact-checker found a major problem that was never fixed. The status leaves out WHO's Oct 10 report that Russian authorities said the death was not due to plague, and the captions leave it out too. In a video about plague testing, that missing development could mislead viewers about the case. Two other fixes were also not applied: the captions still describe the epidemiologic link too broadly ("known case or exposure"), and CDC's "start treatment as soon as suspected" is presented without saying it's guidance for clinicians, so it can read as advice to viewers.

notes: Caption 'AS OF OCTOBER TENTH,' ends on a trailing comma instead of a complete phrase.
The red circular icon at 13.2s is clipped by the right frame edge.
Captions 'WHO NO CASE' and 'ON THE PATIENT' are confusing fragments that don't read as a clear sentence at a glance.
Frame has only tiny icons (microscope, vial, clipboard) clustered in one corner with large empty background, under the ~25% hero-coverage guideline.
Caption 'EXPOSURE CAN'T BE' ends on the dangling word 'BE', leaving the sentence unfinished on screen.
Caption 'INCLUDING F1,' ends on a trailing comma.
Caption 'PATIENT WITH NO' ends on the word 'NO', directly violating the rule against ending captions on a negation.
Test-tube mascot icon in the top right is cropped by the frame edge.
Automated audit confirms text-over-text overlap at 61.37s and 66.25s ('Culture / Lab confirmation means' and 'Culture / and checked by a').
Caption 'AND CHECKED BY A' ends on the dangling article 'A', unfinished mid-sentence.
Caption 'OR A FOURFOLD' is cut off mid-phrase, missing its noun ('rise' or 'change').
Caption 'ROUTE NEEDS A SECOND' cuts off before finishing the thought (missing 'sample'/'test').
Caption 'POSSIBLE EXPOSURE,' ends on a trailing comma.
The mandatory safety line is fragmented into the caption 'OR LOCAL HEALTH', repeating a previously flagged bug where this exact disclaimer gets split across frames.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right in the target window under voice (-13.5 dB) and only slightly hot in pauses (-12.8 vs ~-14), so a gentle -0.9 dB trim (0.9x) tightens both without losing the felt presence. Three cues (i11, i53, i63 swells, with their paired ticks) rendered 20-50 dB under voice — almost inaudible — so they're boosted to carry the "Reported to WHO," "Culture + second test," and "4-fold+/treatment" transition beats; everything else nearby was thinned to stay under the 3-4-effects-per-second rule (redundant whoosh/tick duplicates zeroed at i6,18,37,44,69,74,79,82,87). A few cues spiked close to voice level during speech (i66 pop at -4.6 dB, i77 blip at -7.8 dB, i59/89/90 swooshes) and were pulled down into the -14 to -20 dB speech-SFX zone. Added three bespoke stings — an opening tension pulse, a lab-click at the culture/second-test reveal, and a soft reassuring heartbeat under "treatment starts on suspicion" — to underline the story's emotional beats without stock-kit clutter.

issues.claim: CDC's 2020 case definition treats PCR/antigen tests (incl. F1) as presumptive; confirmation needs a culture plus second test, or a fourfold or greater change in F1 antibodies across 2 blood samples, and that takes time.
